idiom_name: owned return types (Box/Rc/Arc, impl Trait) + Drop; pool guards hand back on drop (PooledConnection)
implementation_notes: Ownership transfer is Rust's core semantics, so the return type already carries the hand-back: a factory returns an owned value (Box/Rc/Arc, impl Trait or the concrete type), the borrow checker prevents the caller from duplicating or forgetting it, and Drop runs the release on every exit path including unwinding. When the resource belongs to a manager, return a guard whose Drop hands it back - r2d2 documents that a pooled connection 'will be returned to the pool when it falls out of scope', and that pooled-connection guard type is the shape to copy - rather than exposing the pool. The classic C++ structure is absorbed by the language; the design decisions left are which ownership shape (single owner versus Rc/Arc) and whether the guard is Send/Sync. A hand-back that must be fallible or asynchronous cannot live in Drop and needs an explicit close on top of the guard.
pitfalls: Drop cannot be called explicitly and cannot be async or fallible: a hand-back that must await (async pool) or report an error needs an explicit close() with Drop as a best-effort backstop.
Escape hatches defeat the guarantee silently - mem::forget, Box::leak, ManuallyDrop and mem::replace on guards remove the hand-back; treat them as unsafe-adjacent and review them.
Rc/Arc cycles keep the resource alive and unreturned: a guard holding an Arc to its pool, or two handles referring to each other, never reach Drop.
A panic inside Drop during unwinding aborts the process (double panic), so pooled release must be panic-free.
